nameStory: The plumose anemone gets its name from its feathery, plume-like tentacles that wave gracefully in the current like an elegant feather duster. The word 'plumose' comes from the Latin 'pluma,' meaning feather, perfectly describing the soft, delicate appearance of this sea anemone's crown of tentacles.
description: The plumose anemone is a large, striking sea anemone that looks like an underwater flower with hundreds of delicate, feathery tentacles. These marine animals attach themselves to rocks, pier pilings, and other hard surfaces in cold ocean waters. They can grow quite large, with their tentacle crown spreading several inches across, and their column-like body stretching up to 6 inches tall. Despite their flower-like appearance, they're actually animals that capture small fish and plankton with their tentacles.

idTips.label: Feathery tentacle crown
idTips.description: Hundreds of fine, delicate tentacles that feel soft and silky to the touch, swaying gracefully like feathers in the current

idTips.label: Smooth column body
idTips.description: A tall, cylindrical body that feels smooth and somewhat squishy, often white, cream, or pale orange in color

idTips.label: Large size
idTips.description: One of the larger anemones in New England waters, with tentacle crowns that can span your open hand

idTips.label: Attachment to hard surfaces
idTips.description: Always found firmly attached to rocks, dock pilings, or shells with a sticky base that grips tightly

idTips.label: Response to touch
idTips.description: Quickly contracts into a tight, wrinkled ball when disturbed, then slowly reopens over several minutes

habitat: Plumose anemones live in cold New England waters, typically found in deeper tide pools, on rocky shores below the low tide line, and attached to pier pilings and dock structures. They prefer areas with good water circulation and are commonly seen by divers and snorkelers in depths from just below low tide to over 100 feet deep. Look for them in harbors around Boston, along the Maine coast, and in protected bays where they attach to any available hard surface.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters begin to warm, with tentacles fully extended for feeding on increasing plankton. This is when they're easiest to spot and photograph.
seasonality.summer: At their most impressive size with full tentacle displays. Warm weather makes tide pool and shallow water exploration most comfortable for observation.
seasonality.fall: Still active and feeding heavily before winter, though tentacles may contract more frequently as water temperatures drop and storms increase.
seasonality.winter: Often contracted during harsh weather but still present. Hardy individuals remain active in deeper, more protected waters throughout the cold season.

funFact: Plumose anemones can live for over 80 years and some individuals may be well over 100 years old, meaning the anemone you're looking at today might have been growing on that same rock since before your grandparents were born!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with frilled anemones, but plumose anemones are much larger and have many more fine, feathery tentacles rather than the thicker, fewer tentacles of frilled anemones. Remember: plumose equals plume-like and plenty of tentacles!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the same species name (Metridium senile), genetic studies have shown that Atlantic and Pacific populations are actually different species, with our New England populations now properly called Metridium dianthus. The word 'senile' in the old scientific name doesn't mean old or decrepit - it refers to the mature, fully-developed tentacle crown.
compareHints: As the only Metridium species in New England waters, plumose anemones are most similar to other large anemones in the region like the northern red anemone. However, plumose anemones have hundreds of fine, feathery tentacles compared to the thicker, fewer tentacles of red anemones, and they're typically white or cream-colored rather than red or green.
